title: Naming the Wall
passage:
Anyone who has stood in front of a paint display has noticed that the names are not descriptions. The trade calls them handles, and at Bellamy & Roe the handles for a season's forty shades are settled last, after the pigments are fixed, by two people with a spreadsheet and one rule. The rule is that a handle must not be checkable. Harbor Fog cannot be held up beside a harbor fog and found wrong; Tomato can, and a customer who grows tomatoes will say so at the counter. So the winners drift toward places nobody has been and weather nobody has photographed. The occasional literal name survives only because the thing it borrows from comes in enough versions to swallow the error — brick, ash, sand.
— Odile Brennan, design notebook

questions.prompt: What are we told about the rule that Bellamy & Roe apply when naming a shade?

options.text: That a name is tested on real customers before the season's pigments are finally settled.
That a name is chosen because no buyer is in a position to prove it inaccurate.
That a name works best when it describes the shade closely enough to be recognized.
That a name is kept only if it can be defended against the trade's own color standards.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, joining the stated rule to the worked example that explains it. The text gives the rule as 'a handle must not be checkable' and then shows what that means in practice: Harbor Fog 'cannot be held up beside a harbor fog and found wrong', whereas Tomato can, and a customer who grows tomatoes 'will say so at the counter'. B paraphrases that. A = wrong order of operations: the passage states the opposite sequence — handles are 'settled last, after the pigments are fixed' — and no customer testing of any kind is described, though pre-launch testing is a plausible thing a paint firm might do. C = the naive general belief the passage opens by denying ('the names are not descriptions'); it is the position a reader brings to the text rather than one the text supports, and the whole rule works the other way round. D = surface_word_match on 'checkable' with the wrong auditor: the passage's test is whether a customer can catch the name out, not whether the name survives an industry color standard, and no such standard is mentioned anywhere. Hedge balance: all four options are confident, unhedged claims and the key is the specific one, so 'pick the qualified answer' does not locate it; D carries the only absolutizer ('only') and is wrong, and the key is not the longest option.
